narrative:
The model estimates a 61% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors that, in combination, signal a higher risk of departure compared to colleagues who are expected to stay.

The strongest influence comes from the fact that you have received other job opportunities while at your current employer. Unlike most employees predicted to stay—where only about 23% report receiving such offers—this stands out as the top factor pushing the prediction toward leaving, as external options often make people more likely to move on.

Next, the number of training programs you attended in the last three years (1-3) also contributes noticeably toward predicting you will leave. While this is fairly common, it appears the model sees limited training engagement as reducing long-term attachment compared to those who either had none or participated much more extensively.

Your overall years of experience (6-10 years) ranks third and similarly nudges the outcome toward leaving. Although this experience level is shared by about 35% of those expected to stay, the model interprets it, alongside the other factors, as indicating you may be at a career stage where changing employers becomes more appealing.

The organization should discuss your external opportunities openly and explore whether additional responsibilities, targeted development, or adjustments to your role could increase your sense of commitment. You might also reflect on what would make staying feel like the clearer choice. (248 words)
